name: Face powder translucent

card.summary: A colorless, finely milled powder that sets makeup and absorbs oil to give a matte, smoother-looking skin finish.
card.note: Overuse can look thick or cakey, and heavy powder on camera can cause visible white patches.

quick.overview:
Translucent face powder is a loose or pressed powder that adds little or no color. Wikipedia describes face powder as a cosmetic used to set makeup, control shine and conceal blemishes, and describes translucent powder as one that mattifies the skin.[1]

For appearance, it reduces oil shine on the forehead, nose and chin and softens the look of pores and fine lines. Men who use light makeup or simply want less shine in photos and video use it because it does not add a visible tint.
quick.how: It is typically applied with a brush or puff, either over foundation and concealer to set them or on bare skin where oil shows through. A technique called baking presses powder under the eyes and on the T-zone, leaves it briefly, then brushes it off for a creaseless finish.[1] Effects last until oil builds back up, usually within hours.
quick.risks: Powders can look heavy or clotted when over-applied.[1] Common ingredients include silica, starch, talc, kaolin and zinc oxide; the page notes toxic ingredients are rare in modern powders.[1] Historical powders contained lead, which led to regulation.[1] People with sensitive or very dry skin may find powder emphasizes dryness.

lead: Translucent face powder is a sheer powder, loose or pressed, that sets makeup and absorbs oil without adding noticeable color.[1] Its aim is a matte, even-looking complexion with less shine.

Face powder in general is listed as serving to absorb oil, set foundation and concealer, conceal blemishes, brighten the complexion and support contouring; finishing powders are used last to minimize the look of fine lines and pores.[1] Powders have a long history, from Egyptian cosmetics to Hollywood-era mass-market compacts, and men's use grew in the 21st century according to the same source.[1]

chain: Makeup is set and shine reduced
Matte, smoother-looking skin in person and on camera
angle.text: Powder is dusted over the T-zone or the whole face to remove shine and blur pores. It changes how the skin surface reflects light for the day rather than changing the skin itself.

infobox: Silica, starch, talc, kaolin, zinc oxide[1]
Set makeup, control shine, soften pores
HD powder, finishing powder, mineral powder[1]

paras: Loose powder is fine and usually sold in a jar, giving light coverage and oil absorption; pressed powder is compacted into a travel-friendly compact and gives more coverage.[1] Translucent powder comes in either form and is described as mattifying.[1]
HD powders are formulated for film and video to reduce shine without leaving white patches under flash, and mineral powders use ground minerals such as iron oxide, talc, zinc and titanium dioxide.[1]
Besides setting makeup, powder is applied directly to skin to reduce shine. The baking technique presses powder under the eyes and on the T-zone before brushing off for a smooth finish.[1]

Wikipedia traces face powder to ancient Egypt, with lead-based powders in Greece, Rome and Renaissance Europe, zinc oxide in the Victorian era, and mass-market adoption in the 1920s and 1930s, followed by Max Factor's Creme Puff in the 1950s.[1] Lead concerns contributed to the 1938 US Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.[1]

timeline.event: US Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act passed, partly in response to concerns over lead in cosmetics.[1]
Max Factor's Creme Puff becomes one of the first all-in-one multipurpose powders.[1]
